raw_text:
# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

### Introduction and Clinical Rationale
The rapid evolution of structural heart interventions, notably transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), has revolutionized valvular heart disease management. While standard transfemoral (TF) arterial access is the gold standard [1], a significant cohort of patients with severe, calcified, or small-caliber iliofemoral arteries are ineligible due to the risk of vascular complications [1,22]. Traditional alternative routes, such as transapical or direct transaortic approaches, avoid iliofemoral anatomy but require thoracotomy and general anesthesia, and are linked to higher morbidity, mortality, and longer hospital stays [21,22]. 

To overcome these challenges, fully percutaneous extrathoracic alternatives have emerged [22]. Among these, transcaval (caval-aortic) access has gained prominence as a versatile percutaneous technique [1]. This approach involves traversing the retroperitoneal space from the inferior vena cava (IVC) into the abdominal aorta to introduce large-bore sheaths [1,3]. It leverages a unique retroperitoneal physiological principle: because the retroperitoneal space is not surgically exposed, it remains pressurized; any aortic bleeding immediately decompresses into the low-pressure IVC rather than expanding into the retroperitoneum [1,3].

### Anatomy, Pre-procedural Planning, and Crossing Technique
The clinical translation of transcaval access was preceded by rigorous preclinical validation in animal models [2] and detailed anatomic suitability analyses [20]. Central to procedural success is meticulous pre-procedural planning using multidetector computed tomography (CT) [5]. CT imaging identifies a "calcium-free window" on the infrarenal abdominal aorta directly facing a vein-free zone of the IVC, typically at the level of the L3/L4 vertebrae [5,20]. It is crucial to map this window relative to the renal arteries and the aortic bifurcation to avoid major branch injury [1,20]. 

During the procedure, an electrified 0.014-inch guidewire is advanced from a catheter positioned in the IVC, crossing the retroperitoneal gap into a target snare pre-positioned in the abdominal aorta via a secondary arterial access [1,3,10]. To facilitate crossing in highly calcified or resistant vessels, operators have successfully employed laser-assisted techniques [26]. Once the wire is snared and externalized, it is exchanged for a stiff wire, allowing the insertion of a large-bore sheath across the caval-aortic tract, through which retrograde interventions can be safely performed [1,3,30].

### Clinical Outcomes in Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement (TAVR)
The safety and efficacy of transcaval TAVR were robustly established in the landmark National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute (NHLBI) prospective, multi-center Investigational Device Exemption (IDE) trial [4]. In 100 high-risk patients, the trial demonstrated a 99% access success rate and a 98% successful tract closure [4]. Importantly, no deaths were directly attributable to transcaval access, and patients experienced a remarkably short length of stay, comparable to standard TF-TAVR [4,11]. Multi-center European registries have corroborated these findings, reporting high technical success and acceptable rates of major vascular complications and life-threatening bleeding [9]. 

Furthermore, clinical outcomes of transcaval TAVR compare favorably with other non-femoral alternative options. A large, propensity-weighted analysis demonstrated that transcaval TAVR is associated with a five-fold lower rate of stroke and a significantly higher rate of direct discharge to home compared to transaxillary access [7]. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses pooling data across several observational cohorts have confirmed that transcaval access is non-inferior to other alternative accesses, with a procedural success rate exceeding 94% and a temporal trend demonstrating declining vascular complications as operator experience matures [12,13]. Notably, transcaval access has successfully expanded TAVR eligibility to challenging populations, including the morbidly obese [27], those with small aortas [29], and patients with pre-existing abdominal aortic grafts, in whom sheaths can be advanced across polyester or endograft structures [14,15]. Furthermore, newer centers with no prior experience have successfully initiated safe programs using this technique [28].

### Beyond TAVR: Mechanical Circulatory Support and Endovascular Interventions
While TAVR remains the primary indication, the utility of transcaval access has expanded to other large-bore structural and endovascular interventions [1,17]. Transcaval access provides a critical portal for delivering temporary percutaneous mechanical circulatory support (MCS) in patients presenting with cardiogenic shock [1,23]. Microaxial flow pumps, such as the Impella 5.0, require large-bore sheaths (up to 23 Fr) that cannot be accommodated by diseased peripheral arteries [28]. The safety and feasibility of delivering these pumps via the transcaval route have been successfully demonstrated, avoiding surgical cutdowns and limb ischemia in critically ill patients [23,28]. Furthermore, complete venous access can be utilized to achieve biventricular mechanical support using venous and transcaval-aortic approaches [25]. Transcaval access has also facilitated left atrial venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (LAVA-ECMO) without pre-procedural contrast CT planning in emergent scenarios [24], as well as thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR) in patients with hostile iliofemoral anatomy [16].

Additionally, the caval-aortic path has been utilized by vascular surgeons for targeted endovascular therapies, most notably transcaval embolization (TCE) for persistent type II endoleaks after endovascular aneurysm repair (EVAR) [17,19]. By establishing an electrosurgical tract from the IVC directly into the excluded aneurysm sac, operators can selectively embolize the feeding vessels or the nidus, providing a highly effective alternative when translumbar or transarterial routes fail [18,19].

### Hemostasis and Tract Closure
Tract closure is a critical phase of the transcaval procedure. Upon completion of the structural intervention, the large-bore sheath is partially withdrawn, and the caval-aortic puncture site is typically closed using off-label, commercially available nitinol cardiac occluders, such as the Amplatzer Duct Occluder (ADO) [1,4]. The 12-month follow-up of the NHLBI study demonstrated excellent long-term durability of this closure method, with a 93% spontaneous fistula occlusion rate at one year and no late vascular complications or adverse clinical sequelae related to the persistent tract [6]. To overcome the challenges associated with off-label devices, a dedicated double-disc nitinol Transcaval Closure Device (TCD) was developed and underwent early feasibility testing [8]. The TCD achieves 100% fistula closure at 30 days, effectively eliminating residual shunting and further simplifying the closure process [8].

### Conclusion
In conclusion, transcaval access has emerged as a secure, fully percutaneous, and reproducible alternative to surgical transapical or transaortic access for structural and endovascular interventions. Guided by meticulous CT planning and robust electrosurgical techniques, it significantly reduces neurological events compared to other alternative accesses and has been endorsed by expert consensus guidelines as a vital alternative for patients with prohibitive vascular anatomy [1,22].
